newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibia bars protests without police permission.
newsitem.headline: Namibia bars protests without police permission.

text.p: Namibian President Sam Nujoma has decreed that no public protests will be allowed without written permission from the police after demonstrations by unemployed former guerrillas.

"No citizens of the Republic of Namibia will be allowed from now on to hold illegal public demonstrations without the approval and written permission by the authority of the Namibian police," Nujoma said in an announcement on public television and radio on Wednesday night.

The decree, Nujoma's first since 1990 independence, follows demonstrations by former combatants of the People's Liberation Army of Namibia (PLAN), who on Tuesday held regional councillors from Nujoma's ruling South West Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO) hostage in Oshakati for several hours as part of a demand for jobs.
The protest went ahead despite the government's promise a week ago that over 4,000 jobs would be found for ex-combatants.
"No person or member of society has the right to attack physically, molest, hold hostage or interfere with other citizens, as happened at Oshakati on the 8th of July," the president said.

"That type of behaviour is violating the laws of Namibia, which clearly state that the citizens have the right to hold peaceful demonstrations, but they should not use violence and endanger the lives of other members of society."
Nujoma said his decree was not aimed at curbing the rights of political parties or trade unions to voice their grievances, but to ensure the safety of ordinary citizens.
"I want to make it abundantly clear that political parties have the freedom to organise, politicise, campaign and recruit members from society," he added.
Nujoma did not specify actions to be taken against those who staged public demonstrations without the approval of the police.
The Legal Assistance Centre (LAC) in Windhoek said the decree was unconstitutional.
"We are unable to find any law requiring persons to notify and obtain the approval of the Namibian Police before holding a demonstration or procession", it said in a statement.
"Any law that did would be in violation of the constitutional right to assemble peacefully," the centre added.
The LAC said freedom to associate, demonstrate and protest was vital in any democracy and had so far been respected by the Namibian government.
